name: Pick and Place Machine

claims.claim_text: A surface-mount assembly line is a sequence of physically separate machines joined by a conveyor: solder-paste application, pick and place, reflow oven, and automated optical inspection, with the board entering at one end and emerging assembled at the other.
claims.quote_verbatim: then it goes into the reflow oven, and then to the automated visual inspection

claims.claim_text: The stencil printer aligns the stencil apertures to the board and prints solder paste, a slurry of tacky flux and powdered solder; the pick-and-place machine then uses vacuum to lift components from feeders and set them into the paste, whose tackiness holds them in position until reflow melts the solder.
claims.quote_verbatim: And the paste is sticky and tacky. So those parts don't go anywhere.
claims.speaker: Chris Denney

claims.claim_text: Because the board travels the line on a conveyor, a production panel needs a strip along its outer edge carrying sprocket holes, which the conveyor rails and the bed-of-nails tester use to advance and align it.
claims.quote_verbatim: you need the holes on the outer edge of the board

claims.claim_text: Test coupons and manufacturing strips added top and bottom of a panel carry the sprocket holes that let the assembly machines take the board through the line, which is part of design for manufacture rather than an electrical requirement.
claims.quote_verbatim: the socket holes in them that allow your pick and place machine to take your board through

claims.claim_text: In a well-run assembly shop the only manual steps are loading the board at the head of the conveyor, an inspector between placement and reflow who looks for catastrophic faults without touching the board, and through-hole insertion; through-hole placement has resisted automation while functional test is normally fixtured and automatic.
claims.quote_verbatim: I haven't seen any automated through hole stuff
claims.speaker: Zach Hoeken
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Zach Hoeken Smith - Creative China Commorant

claims.claim_text: Design for manufacture review for an assembled board checks clearance between parts for the placement head and whether heavy parts sit on the side that must pass through the process twice; at quantities of ten or twenty a shop can jig around such faults, while at five hundred the review governs whether the board must be laid out again.
claims.quote_verbatim: Is there, is there clearance between the parts so that the pick and place head, are they too close together?
claims.episode_title: Electronics Manufacturing History with David Ray

claims.claim_text: Feeders, not the motion system, are what make a machine a pick and place: a gantry with a vacuum head and no tape feeders cannot run jelly-bean parts continuously and is therefore no faster than hand placement.
claims.quote_verbatim: It is not a pick and place until you've got tape feeders. You have to have tape feeders.

claims.claim_text: The cost of a placement machine is concentrated in the feeding mechanism and the vision system rather than the XY motion, which is why the class of machine that reliably takes components off reels starts around ten thousand dollars.
claims.quote_verbatim: There's a reason why these machines cost upwards of $10,000 is because they're complicated.
claims.episode_title: Analog Devices, Design Spark - Unusual Usenet Usurpation

claims.claim_text: Feeders are typically the most expensive consumable part of an assembly line, on the order of five hundred dollars each, and an assembly house wants as many as possible because a part already sitting in a feeder removes setup time from every job that uses it.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's, like, at least $500 a feeder

claims.claim_text: Feeder count sets the number of passes a board needs. If the machine cannot hold every unique part at once the board must be run through a second or third time, which removes the machine's time advantage over hand placement.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you don't have enough feeders to handle all the components you need, then you've got to go for a second or a third run through
claims.episode_title: Shop bots, 450 mm fabs & redFrog - Pick and Place Palillogy

claims.claim_text: A typical machine carries somewhere between twenty and forty reel positions, so the number of unique parts on a board, not the number of placements, is the quantity that determines setup cost; adding one part past the machine's slot count forces a second setup.
claims.quote_verbatim: pick-and-place can be anywhere from 20 to 40 reels
claims.episode_title: Last Minute Decisions - Obdurate Onepercenter Obstacles

claims.claim_text: Designers reduce the unique-part count on a bill of materials specifically to stay within the assembler's feeder capacity, because keeping a board at twenty reels instead of twenty-one avoids a changeover.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you get to 20 reels instead of 21 on your, and you don't have to do a change, then you, you win.
claims.episode_title: FPGAs, Robots & Thermocouples - Wampum's Wavering Worth

claims.claim_text: Unconsolidated passive values consume feeder capacity quickly: a board carrying around sixty distinct resistor types would fill a typical machine with resistors alone.
claims.quote_verbatim: I think it was like 60 different types. And it was like, and that would fill up a pick and place machine.
claims.episode_title: Two and a Half Orders of Magnitude

claims.claim_text: A machine populated with sixty feeders cannot place a sixty-one part board in a single pass, so a bill of materials that lists more uniques than the machine has slots costs an extra pass even when the extra part is trivial.
claims.quote_verbatim: if machines haven't got 60 feeders, I've done a video on this, you know, and, and you've got 61 parts

claims.claim_text: An integrated part that replaces a discrete circuit is bought partly for feeder economics: one reel on the machine instead of four is a direct reduction in setup and slot pressure.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's a single reel on your pick and place machine instead of four reels

claims.claim_text: Reusing a higher-rated part already loaded on the line rather than specifying the exactly correct lower-rated one is normal practice, because a second reel occupying a feeder slot for one component is more expensive than the part difference.
claims.quote_verbatim: you don't want to have a reel of components on your pick and place machine for the one in 4001s just for the battery

claims.claim_text: Newer feeders accept loose cut tape, so a customer can order the exact quantity of a part from a distributor rather than a full reel and the assembler does not have to re-reel it.
claims.quote_verbatim: It can, uh, it can take a loose tape
claims.episode_title: Chris Becomes Self Employed - Quixotic Quitting Quaere

claims.claim_text: Short cut-tape strips from distributors carry a leader, and a machine will consume a substantial fraction of a ten-part strip before it places reliably, so buying exact quantities of expensive parts for machine placement can waste most of them.
claims.quote_verbatim: But then the machine ends up just wasting half of them anyway.

claims.claim_text: An assembler must be supplied with more components than the board count requires, because winding a reel onto the machine loses parts at the start of the run; expensive components should be flagged so the shop handles them carefully rather than treating them as attrition.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can't give your manufacturer a reel of 100 resistors and expect them to populate 100 boards
claims.episode_title: Solar Cells, SparkFun, TSMC - The Detroit Debunking

claims.claim_text: In one high-volume factory the machine's dropped parts were collected at the end of each shift and returned to reels; this is normal cost discipline and usually harmless, but a lead bent in the drop will produce a part that no longer mounts flush.
claims.quote_verbatim: at the end of the shift, somebody picks up all those parts and then they go back on reels
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer

claims.claim_text: The feeder behaves as a smart cartridge that completes the machine: it carries identifying data about what part it holds and what it is doing, so the machine knows the contents of each slot without separate programming.
claims.quote_verbatim: It may not necessarily have a microchip on it, but it's got something that says, you know, this is what I am
claims.speaker: Chris Denney

claims.claim_text: Two alignment technologies are used: a camera and a laser. Components sit loose in the tape pocket and are never picked exactly centred, so the machine must measure what it actually holds; one method rotates the part ninety degrees past a laser line to derive both the angular and the XY offset and corrects for them at placement.
claims.quote_verbatim: it'll actually turn it 90 degrees and it uses like a laser line to basically measure it
claims.speaker: Ryan O'Hara
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ryan O'Hara - Keyed, Kerfed Kapton

claims.claim_text: A through-axis camera that looks along the nozzle is the feature that separates a working machine from a toy, because without it there is no way to see what the vacuum pickup is holding in order to align it.
claims.quote_verbatim: You want to, a through axis camera.
claims.speaker: Ryan O'Hara
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ryan O'Hara - Keyed, Kerfed Kapton

claims.claim_text: Cheap machines substitute stepper motors for the closed-loop positioning that placement accuracy requires; good encoders are what make a machine accurate and they are expensive, so the sub-five-thousand-dollar capable machine remains out of reach.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're trying to use stepper motors to do things that you really need a closed loop system for
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jonathan Hirschman of PCB:NG

claims.claim_text: Most placement machines work natively in metric and convert Imperial input, so a design submitted in inches accumulates cascading rounding errors through the conversion.
claims.quote_verbatim: most of the pick-and-place machines out there, you know, speak metric natively
claims.speaker: Jonathan Hirschman
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jonathan Hirschman of PCB:NG

claims.claim_text: Placement machines are specified against the wrong problem: the published specifications describe capabilities that are not the ones that determine whether a given job runs correctly.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're typically designed to have really great specs. But those specs are geared towards the wrong problem
claims.speaker: Jonathan Hirschman
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jonathan Hirschman of PCB:NG

claims.claim_text: Reliable picking is tuned per component: nozzle dwell time on the exposed tape pocket, suction level, and release timing are all separately adjustable, and each has to be set for each part type.
claims.quote_verbatim: how long do you actually linger on it
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: If the Z height is set wrong the head presses harder than intended and parts are flung off the board rather than placed; height and placement pressure are the same adjustment in practice.
claims.quote_verbatim: If your height's not set correctly, you push down harder.

claims.claim_text: On a run of roughly twelve hundred identical LEDs a desktop machine placed about ninety-five percent correctly with little setup; the residual failure was parts landing on their side, which the vision system did not reject because the lens made the part outline non-square and it failed to recognise the wrong-side silhouette.
claims.quote_verbatim: I had a lot of them where they were actually flipping up on their side
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Better machines allow the placement force to be programmed, which matters because delicate parts, such as some capacitors, have their leads damaged if the head sets them down too hard.
claims.quote_verbatim: on the good pick-and-place machines, you can adjust how much force it puts them down with
claims.episode_title: Capacitors, Simulation and Closures - Deonerated Design Dealmaking

claims.claim_text: On a desktop machine running a batch of five hundred boards, an error that halts the run occurs on roughly one board in ten, or about one placement in a few hundred; the usual causes are the vacuum head sitting on the part badly or the upward-facing camera finding a silhouette that does not match the expected part size or orientation.
claims.quote_verbatim: maybe like one out of every 10 boards, maybe like one out of every few hundred placements
claims.speaker: David Ray
claims.episode_title: Electronics Manufacturing History with David Ray

claims.claim_text: A machine can be set to abandon a part after several consecutive vision failures, complete everything else on the board, and report the omissions at the end, so a single bad feeder does not stop the run ten minutes in and waste the remaining hours.
claims.quote_verbatim: if it gets like three missed picks in a row that say fail vision
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: The placement machine has no way of knowing whether the reel loaded into a slot is the part it was told to expect; a wrong-value reel is a common fault and is caught only downstream at automated optical inspection, which compares each board against a photographed golden reference and can read the marking on the component.
claims.quote_verbatim: the pick and place machine assumes that you've put the correct part in the correct slot. It doesn't know

claims.claim_text: Roughly half the labour of populating boards is loading the correct components into the correct feeders, and a mix-up such as a ten-kilohm resistor in the slot programmed for a one-hundred-nanofarad capacitor is catastrophic for the whole run.
claims.quote_verbatim: that goes along with populating boards and the pick and place is just putting the correct resistors in the right reels
claims.episode_title: An Interview with the SparkFun Team - Efficacious Engineering Ensemble

claims.claim_text: Some low-cost machines reference the board from the first component's position rather than from fiducials, which changes the setup procedure compared with fiducial-based alignment.
claims.quote_verbatim: they have this really weird method of like component one is your zero, zero
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Fiducial support is a differentiator among low-cost machines: one sub-three-thousand-dollar model supports only a single fiducial, which limits how far board scale and rotation can be corrected.
claims.quote_verbatim: it only supported one fiducial
claims.episode_title: Picking a Pick and Place Pickiness

claims.claim_text: Setting up a machine for a new board requires a pilot production run to confirm that the program, the part orientations and the rest of the configuration are correct before committing to the batch.
claims.quote_verbatim: You have to do a little pilot production run to make sure everything's programmed right and all the orientation's correct
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Fabienne Serrière of KnitYak

claims.claim_text: Every placement machine handles 0603 as a baseline, but 0402 is a discontinuity: it requires different, smaller nozzles, not all machines can do it, and yield falls, so a design should not go below 0603 without a reason.
claims.quote_verbatim: Every pick-and-place machine will do 0603 as a minimum. But then there's a bit of a jump to the 0402s.
claims.episode_title: Ceramic capacitors & High end scopes - Kempt Kickstarter Kakorrhaphiophobia

claims.claim_text: Going below 0402 to 0201 requires smaller nozzle heads again, which not every assembler owns; a shop that must buy nozzles for one customer's job will charge the tooling back as non-recurring engineering.
claims.quote_verbatim: So, some pick and place machines aren't capable of going the 0402 route.

claims.claim_text: Package choice is a filter on how many suppliers can build the board: at 0805 any machine will do the work, 0402 cuts the available machines to roughly sixty-five percent, and 0201 to roughly thirty percent.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's now down to 65% of all the machines and 0201, 30% of the machines

claims.claim_text: A machine specified for 0201 may not achieve it in daily production, because motor repeatability at that precision is not the same thing as placing real parts from real feeders every day; a machine that has only ever been run on larger passives by its existing customers has not been proved at the small end.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's a difference between a motor, like precision that can get to that, to that, that repeatability
claims.speaker: Joe Garrison
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Joe and Mark Garrison - Subtly Spelling SayLeeAy

claims.claim_text: Even where a machine can place 0201, it may do so slowly enough to matter: the precision mode can add on the order of eighty percent to the time per board, which does not show up in the placement specification.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you have to take, you know, 80% more time per board
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Joe and Mark Garrison - Subtly Spelling SayLeeAy

claims.claim_text: Before buying, have the actual production board built on the exact machine under consideration, and insist on speaking to customers running the same package mix daily rather than the reference customers the vendor offers; a machine selected for a hard package mix should be one contract manufacturers use in production.
claims.quote_verbatim: to have that board built by the machine, by that exact machine before you buy it
claims.speaker: Joe Garrison
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Joe and Mark Garrison - Subtly Spelling SayLeeAy

claims.claim_text: Choosing the smallest possible packages to minimise board area constrains manufacturing at both ends: it narrows which machines can be bought and it rules out many contract manufacturers.
claims.quote_verbatim: not only on your own, but when you go to a contract manufacturer as well, that rules out many contract manufacturers
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Joe and Mark Garrison - Subtly Spelling SayLeeAy

claims.claim_text: A panel must be sized to the assembler's machine, not to the PCB fabricator's maximum panel. Fabricators quote panels in inches, commonly eighteen by twenty-four, and panels of that size frequently do not fit a placement machine.
claims.quote_verbatim: Panels are large. The panels that they order from the manufacturers, they are large and often they will not fit in pick and place machines.

claims.claim_text: Board width, not length, is usually the binding limit, because boards feed lengthwise through the machine on rails; one desktop machine offers about four hundred millimetres of total span and its rails cannot be set to the extreme edges.
claims.quote_verbatim: It has, I think 400 millimeters total space across and the rails can't go all the way to the edges

claims.claim_text: A large panel held only at its edge rails will bow when the head presses down, and a V-grooved or slot-routed panel of that size can fold or snap in half at the first placement.
claims.quote_verbatim: Your board will just snap in half as soon as the head hits it.

claims.claim_text: Panelisation should be agreed with the assembler before the boards are fabricated, since a panel that does not fit the placement machine is discovered only when the finished panels arrive at the assembly house.
claims.quote_verbatim: Talk to your assembler first because
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Laen - Purple PCB Philosophy

claims.claim_text: A five-hundred-millimetre circular LED display was built as four separate quadrant boards of about two hundred and fifty millimetres square specifically so that each piece would fit the available placement machine.
claims.quote_verbatim: It was like 250mm square board so I could run it on my pick and place.
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: Large-format assembly machines exist that take boards up to about one point six metres in length; they are built as a widened standard machine with two heads that can either run as two independent machines on small boards or both place onto one long board, and they are expensive per board for small work.
claims.quote_verbatim: they can actually do boards up to 1.6 metres
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: A machine whose build area is only Euro-card sized defeats the purpose of automation, because the economic unit a placement machine works on is a panel rather than a single board.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you have to do one board, the whole point of a pick and place machine is that you can do a panel at a time.
claims.episode_title: Contextual Electronics, ClubJameco and Solderpaste - Lifelong Learning Likelihood

claims.claim_text: Owning a placement machine changes layout practice permanently in one respect: every board is panelised from then on, because panelising costs nothing and a machine run on a panel is proportionally cheaper to set up.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's no reason for me never to panelize again

claims.claim_text: The centroid is the reference point the machine picks a part at, so a library footprint whose origin sits on pin one forces the assembler to re-enter a reference point for every such component; the pin-one marker is of no use to the placement program.
claims.quote_verbatim: they've got to change the reference point, the centroid point

claims.claim_text: Placing the origin at the part centroid, which the machine requires, conflicts with layout practice, because the designer works on a placement snap grid and a centred origin leaves the pins off the routing grid.
claims.quote_verbatim: having the centroid in the center of the part is bloody annoying

claims.claim_text: A component type the machine's library has not seen before still requires a person to read the data sheet and enter the part dimensions; this step of the flow has not been automated.
claims.quote_verbatim: it still requires you looking up a data sheet and determining what size that component is
claims.speaker: Chris Denney

claims.claim_text: An in-house computer-aided-manufacturing workflow can analyse the Gerber and pick-and-place files and generate the machine programs directly, with release management and file tracking held in the same system as the rest of the manufacturing data.
claims.quote_verbatim: analyze like Gerber files, pick and place files, and actually create the programs that we run on the pick on our specific Juki pick and place machines
claims.speaker: Luke Beno
claims.episode_title: AI Tooling with Matt Liberty and Luke Beno

claims.claim_text: A streamlined in-house flow keeps the PCB library orientations identical to the tape orientation in the feeders, so a previously used part never has to be checked for rotation when it is placed again.
claims.quote_verbatim: all my PCB library parts are the same way around as the tape in my feeders
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: One short-timescale workflow runs layout first, exports the bill of materials from the board file as the shopping list for parts, boards and stencil, and begins assembly on the in-house machine about two days later.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'll do the board layout. I'll then export the bomb from that board layout to produce the shopping list.
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: The viability of a low-end machine is decided by placements per hour against manual placement, the number and reliability of the feeders, the setup time, and the machine's reliability; the combination leaves only a narrow window in which owning one saves money.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's a very narrow window of where a do-it-yourself pick and place machine makes sense
claims.episode_title: Shop bots, 450 mm fabs & redFrog - Pick and Place Palillogy

claims.claim_text: A machine placing one hundred components an hour is useless: the throughput floor for any placement machine is that it must be at least as quick as doing the job by hand.
claims.quote_verbatim: a pick and place that does 100 components an hour is a waste of time

claims.claim_text: Hand placement runs at roughly three hundred components an hour, which is the figure a desktop machine has to beat; one desktop design claimed twelve hundred and fifty components an hour.
claims.quote_verbatim: 300 components per hour. Oh, sorry, that's by hand

claims.claim_text: On an eight-by-eight panel carrying two hundred and fifty-six parts, hand placement took about half an hour while a single-head machine completed it in under three minutes.
claims.quote_verbatim: this little eight by eight would take me about a half hour to place all the parts by hand. It's 256 parts
claims.speaker: Ryan O'Hara
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ryan O'Hara - Keyed, Kerfed Kapton

claims.claim_text: A run of twelve hundred identical LEDs across a four-up panel took roughly five to ten minutes per board with three placement heads working, about twenty minutes per panel.
claims.quote_verbatim: I think I had three pick heads going
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Setup dominates infrequent use: exporting the position file, converting it to the machine's format and recalling the procedure took two to three hours for one job, principally because the operator does not do it often enough to retain the steps.
claims.quote_verbatim: That was probably two or three hours
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: For a small job the machine setup can exceed the time to place the board by hand, and the arithmetic should be done before the machine is set up rather than after.
claims.quote_verbatim: And in that time, in half that time, you could have just assembled the board yourself.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A rough quantity threshold for setting up a machine is around one hundred boards; at ten boards the setup is not recovered and hand placement is faster.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're doing a hundred boards you know or it might be worth setting up your pick-and-place machine but if you're doing 10 boards
claims.episode_title: Guns and Mobile Labs - Nuanced Nomadic Non-essentials

claims.claim_text: Above roughly one hundred units the case for in-house placement weakens and outside assembly becomes the sensible route; below it, an owner with a heavily optimised flow and repeat clients can beat the turnaround an outside shop will give.
claims.quote_verbatim: But once you get above 100, you know, like why?

claims.claim_text: The purchase decision is an arithmetic comparison against per-board assembly pricing: at roughly five dollars a board to have it assembled outside, a ten-thousand-dollar machine plus the time to learn, run and maintain it needs a large and steady volume to be recovered.
claims.quote_verbatim: let's just say five bucks to assemble a board. You go like, well, how do you justify $10,000 pick and place machine

claims.claim_text: Because programming, reeling and loading are fixed overheads that only pay back over many identical boards, a placement machine is justified by commercial production quantities rather than by prototyping.
claims.quote_verbatim: You're talking production, commercial production quantities.

claims.claim_text: A workshop making batches of about fifty hand-assembles instead, because the barrier is not only the purchase price but the time to learn the machine and the floor space it needs; outsourcing at five to ten pounds a board is cheaper than absorbing both.
claims.quote_verbatim: The cost is it's not just the cost of the pick in place. It's the learning.
claims.speaker: Ian Johnston

claims.claim_text: A machine that is not used at least weekly is a poor allocation of capital compared with other equipment, whatever else it teaches its owner about manufacturing.
claims.quote_verbatim: unless you're using it at least weekly, there may be better things you could be spending your money on
claims.speaker: Dafydd Roche

claims.claim_text: Of the people who believe they need a placement machine, roughly ninety percent do not; the genuine case is low board counts, high product mix and a requirement for fast turnaround, and it is conditional on accepting the time needed to develop the process and software flow.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's probably a 90% chance that you don't

claims.claim_text: The difficulty of running a placement machine is not one large problem but a large number of very small ones, each individually capable of stopping a job, and they are only learned by using a machine.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's not one big problem. It's lots and lots and lots and lots of tiny, tiny issues
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: A machine may sit idle for a month between jobs and still be worth owning where the alternative is subcontractor scheduling, because the small subcontractors that will take short-run work tend to disappear and the large ones will not take it.
claims.quote_verbatim: Sometimes you'll, like, lie idle for a month, then it'll get used to something. But it's absolutely worth it.
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: The subcontractor problem for short runs is structural: very small assembly shops fail when they lose a single customer, large ones will not take small jobs, and a correctly sized one will schedule small jobs around its major customers, with no option to pay a premium for a faster turnaround because the job is not worth their while.
claims.quote_verbatim: the really small ones generally just disappear
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Mike Harrison - X-ray Examining Xenogogue

claims.claim_text: Owning the machine also removes the documentation burden that a subcontractor requires, which for short-timescale one-off work can dominate the job.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you've got to deal with a subcontractor, you've got so much documentation to do
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: Placement equipment fell from roughly half a million dollars to around ten thousand dollars over the period in which small-scale assembly became feasible, which is what put the equipment within reach of small companies and individuals.
claims.quote_verbatim: they don't cost half a million dollars anymore. They cost 10 grand.
claims.episode_title: Open Hardware and The Creative Economy

claims.claim_text: High-end multi-head production machines cost on the order of half a million dollars, and capital equipment for an assembly line at a million dollars a machine is not unusual, with a sales and evaluation cycle running close to a year.
claims.quote_verbatim: a million dollars is not uncommon
claims.speaker: Chris Denney

claims.claim_text: A bare-bones new desktop machine can be had for around ten thousand dollars, but feeders and the surrounding support equipment take the real figure to twenty thousand and upwards; the machines used by the better-known open-hardware companies were around fifty thousand.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can probably get a bare bones one for 10, but by the time you include all the feeders and all the support stuff, yeah, you're going to be paying 20 upwards
claims.episode_title: eReaders, datasheets & board assembly - Yearly Yeasty Yapping

claims.claim_text: Running a machine of that class is a full-time job in itself, so a single-person operation gains nothing from owning one and loses the automation it was bought for.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's a full-time job to maintain and run these things.
claims.episode_title: eReaders, datasheets & board assembly - Yearly Yeasty Yapping

claims.claim_text: Used mid-1990s production machines running DOS remain capable and can be bought in good condition for around ten thousand dollars, with about fifteen thousand covering the machine set up and supported.
claims.quote_verbatim: so you can get one of these odds for like right around 10 K and really good shape
claims.speaker: Ryan O'Hara
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ryan O'Hara - Keyed, Kerfed Kapton

claims.claim_text: A four-thousand-dollar Chinese desktop machine reaches about five to five and a half thousand delivered once shipping and a spare-parts kit are included, and at that point it lacks the vision and alignment capability that would make it useful, so it becomes a five-thousand-dollar white elephant.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can end up buying a $5,000 white elephant
claims.speaker: Ryan O'Hara
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ryan O'Hara - Keyed, Kerfed Kapton

claims.claim_text: A nominally five-thousand-dollar imported machine landed in Australia at about six thousand once postage and currency conversion were counted, which is the same money as a large quantity of assembly time at a professional shop.
claims.quote_verbatim: But six grand buys me an awful lot of assembly time on a professional pick-and-place machine.

claims.claim_text: A genuinely capable machine below five thousand dollars is not achievable, because a machine at that price will not be large enough or structurally rigid enough to carry ten-thousand-part reels.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's not going to probably be big enough or, you know, have the structural integrity to hold, you know, 10,000 components on a big reel
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jonathan Hirschman of PCB:NG

claims.claim_text: A twenty-five-thousand-dollar Japanese desktop machine bought as a used floor model was designed for prototyping rather than manufacturing; production-grade placement means Juki, Panasonic or Samsung equipment.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's from a company called MDC in Tokyo
claims.speaker: Akiba
claims.episode_title: An interview with Akiba from Freaklabs - Dimissory Diagraphical Debt

claims.claim_text: A refurbishment market exists for older production machines: a vendor takes them in, replaces the ageing components such as hard drives with more stable parts, and resells them, which is how a forty-eight-feeder machine reaches a small shop.
claims.quote_verbatim: They basically take these old machines in. They clean them all up.
claims.speaker: Dafydd Roche

claims.claim_text: A Neoden 4 desktop machine carries forty-eight feeders with both up-looking and down-looking vision and places 0402 components, at around ten thousand dollars.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's got 48 feeders on it and it's got up and down vision. It's got, it can do 0402 components.

claims.claim_text: A later model brought a dual-camera, dual-head machine with an automatic tool changer and forty feeders under three thousand dollars, but its feeders are built in rather than removable cassettes, so a feeder cannot be preloaded off the machine or swapped between jobs.
claims.quote_verbatim: They're, they're not removable, uh, cassette feeders.
claims.episode_title: Picking a Pick and Place Pickiness

claims.claim_text: Three low-cost Charmhigh machines can be run in series to cover a bill of materials larger than one machine's feeder capacity, or the same job run on all three in parallel; most jobs have fewer than fifty bill-of-materials lines, and of those a further portion is through-hole or too large for the machine to place.
claims.quote_verbatim: But also like most jobs are going to have less than 50 bomb items.
claims.speaker: David Ray
claims.episode_title: Electronics Manufacturing History with David Ray

claims.claim_text: Assist machines occupy the space between hand and automatic placement: an XY table with a thumb-pressed vacuum head, around sixteen feeders and tube support, moved by the operator's arm, at roughly four thousand dollars.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's basically an X, Y table with like this, uh, manual, like it's got a thumb press on the top

claims.claim_text: Used desktop machines are scarce outside the main markets: in Australia they come through one or two large dealers at around twenty thousand dollars, and a used machine under five thousand is not realistic.
claims.quote_verbatim: you'll be paying 20 grand for one

claims.claim_text: A cheap machine can only take tape feeders, so a board with parts in tubes or trays cannot be fully populated on it; if the machine cannot place every package on the board the case for using it collapses.
claims.quote_verbatim: but then it can't do tubes, right? It can only do feeders
claims.episode_title: Contextual Electronics, ClubJameco and Solderpaste - Lifelong Learning Likelihood

claims.claim_text: Import tariffs of twenty-five percent applied to manufacturing equipment as well as components, changing the delivered price of a desktop placement machine by about twenty-five hundred dollars depending on the order date.
claims.quote_verbatim: he basically saved 2500 bucks

claims.claim_text: A machine left unused still needs maintenance: running it a couple of times a month to move the motors, and storage covered and out of dust, since the linear drives are the part that degrades.
claims.quote_verbatim: he was going to keep it in a location where he could actually run it twice a month

claims.claim_text: Floor space and noise are first-order constraints on owning placement equipment: a full line takes a large amount of room and is loud, and machines have been rejected purely because they would not fit through the door.
claims.quote_verbatim: One of my friends just recently sold an entire pick and place line because it takes up way too much room.
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer

claims.claim_text: Outsourcing at a batch size chosen for unit economics freezes the design until the inventory is consumed; an in-house line making about a hundred units a day removes that constraint and allowed roughly thirty board revisions in a year, each one cheaper or more reliable to build.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can't change the design until you've sold all 1,000 of them
claims.speaker: Chris Anderson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Anderson - Deambulatory Daedal Drones

claims.claim_text: A used Juki bought on eBay for forty thousand dollars, with eighty tape-and-reel feed lines, stick feeders and a tray feeder, was paid for within four months against what the same volume of boards would have cost in subcontractor charges and labour; the surrounding process was a small reflow oven, a manual screen printer, a full stock of reels and a dedicated operator.
claims.quote_verbatim: So we spent $40,000 buying our own pick and place robot.
claims.speaker: Vincent Himpe
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Vincent Himpe - Escaped Electron Elocution

claims.claim_text: One volume threshold used in practice is a hundred to five hundred units built in house on the shop's own machine for speed, with anything above a thousand sent to specialist assembly houses that do nothing else and achieve higher yields.
claims.quote_verbatim: for small batches of, say, 100 and sometimes even 500, Seed will do pick-and-place in-house
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Lesnet - Bus Buccaneer Builder

claims.claim_text: A small manufacturer that makes everything in batches of fifty to a hundred can justify a machine when all its products fit on one set of feeders, because the setup can then be left standing between jobs; the same machine cannot be offered as a service to outside customers, which would destroy that advantage.
claims.quote_verbatim: we could fit all of our products on one set of feeders
claims.speaker: Charles Alexanian

claims.claim_text: A low-cost machine is not a finished tool: it works, but it needs continual attention and each time it is restarted after a gap the operator relearns another of its quirks.
claims.quote_verbatim: each time you fire it back up, you got, you're learning a new cork
claims.speaker: Charles Alexanian

claims.claim_text: Bringing placement in house converts an electrical engineer into a process engineer, whose concerns become solder-paste thickness, placement accuracy to the thousandth of an inch, rotation, and the statistical distribution of placement over time.
claims.quote_verbatim: You become a process engineer. You don't become an electrical engineer.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching" with Davidson and Vandenbout - Presbytes Pushing Portfolios

claims.claim_text: For quantities of two or three pieces the shortest lead time is to build the boards yourself with a tabletop stencil printer and reflow oven, while contract shops that maintain a prototype line remain the route for anything larger.
claims.quote_verbatim: the shortest lead time, if I need two or three pieces of something is to build it myself
claims.speaker: Bob Davidson
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching" with Davidson and Vandenbout - Presbytes Pushing Portfolios

claims.claim_text: Owning a machine feeds back into design: the designer learns to avoid parts that would require a nozzle change and steers component selection by what the machine handles well.
claims.quote_verbatim: having a pick and places definitely made me a better design engineer for manufacturer of parts
claims.speaker: Ryan O'Hara
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ryan O'Hara - Keyed, Kerfed Kapton

claims.claim_text: Automation does not remove labour from assembly so much as change it: loading a placement machine requires organisation and a stockroom, and the facilities that house such machines are of a higher standard than hand-stuffing operations.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's not like it's easy to load up a pick-and-place, right? It's, you know, you need a lot of organization, you need a stock room
claims.episode_title: PCBs, Tektronix & Ham Radio - Habitual Handicraft Hangups

claims.claim_text: The bottleneck on a mixed-job line is set by process mix rather than machine speed: leaded chip parts slow placement while they are validated, bulk passives run fast, and on some jobs reflow is the slowest step.
claims.quote_verbatim: if we're doing a lot of chip parts, I mean, like leaded chip parts, that can slow down quite a bit while it's validating those
claims.speaker: Chris Church
claims.episode_title: An interview with Macrofab - Macro Manufacturing Mechanization

claims.claim_text: Where a job uses the assembler's house-stocked parts, only the few remaining components are hand-placed, at roughly ten seconds per part.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's about 10 seconds per part
claims.speaker: Parker Dillman
claims.episode_title: An interview with Macrofab - Macro Manufacturing Mechanization

claims.claim_text: With a semi-automatic stencil printer the board is loaded by hand and the stencil swap is the slow step, so printer setup can take longer than the placement machine setup for the same job.
claims.quote_verbatim: that takes longer to set that up correctly sometimes than the actual pick-and-place machine
claims.speaker: Parker Dillman
claims.episode_title: An interview with Macrofab - Macro Manufacturing Mechanization

claims.claim_text: Line productivity is decided by the automation around the machines rather than by the machines themselves: buffers, magazines and loaders keep the machine fed and unloaded so nobody has to stand at it, and the economic argument is that machines are cheap relative to people.
claims.quote_verbatim: machines aren't expensive. People are expensive.
claims.speaker: Chris Denney

claims.claim_text: A rolling changeover keeps a line running: the upstream stencil printer is changed over and the next job printed while the placement machines are still finishing the current one, and each placement machine is changed over while the one after it still runs.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're changing over your pick and place while the last pick and place is still running
claims.speaker: Chris Denney

claims.claim_text: A board with around eight hundred and fifty placements drawn from about a hundred and five unique parts cannot be built in one pass on a single machine, so two or three placement machines are run in series after a single paste print.
claims.quote_verbatim: you might have to run for a board that has what? 800 components with a hundred uniques

claims.claim_text: The stated ideal for a contract assembler is that every step from stencil printing through placement and reflow happens without operator intervention, so labour is confined to what arrives and what ships.
claims.quote_verbatim: the pinnacle that we're always trying to achieve is that all those processes happen without people having to do anything
claims.speaker: Chris Denney

claims.claim_text: Even at professional assembly houses operators are commonly seen constantly attending the machines; where the process is correctly set up they should not be, and a well-set-up shop can have one person running three or four machines, which requires either high volume or a predictable repeating schedule with a dedicated bank of feeders per customer.
claims.quote_verbatim: one guy can probably run three or four machines
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: A three-day turnkey assembly service is made possible by constraining the customer to a published parts library: the vendor holds that stock, the parts are already programmed into the feeders, and there is no exposure to outside part delays.
claims.quote_verbatim: Seed Studios just announced a three day turn PCBA, but you have to be using the open parts library
claims.episode_title: Inspirations and Aspirations - Recanting Rocket Rationale

claims.claim_text: Turnkey assemblers price lower for designs built from their suggested parts because those reels are already loaded in their machines; the saving is unavailable to designs whose parts are precision or single-source and cannot be substituted.
claims.quote_verbatim: Because they've already got those reels, you know, lined up in their pick-and-place machines.

claims.claim_text: One assembly service began with the thesis of driving customers onto roughly two thousand common parts and keeping twenty-five to thirty machines permanently loaded with them; the size of the part space defeated it, and the working model instead decouples mass storage of individual parts from the placement step and treats material handling as the central problem.
claims.quote_verbatim: we'll just buy like 25, 30 pick and place machines
claims.speaker: Andrew Seddon
claims.episode_title: CircuitHub, 12 Years Later with Andrew Seddon

claims.claim_text: A desktop open-source machine of the Lumen class is aimed at low to medium volume, specifically in-house prototype batches for teams unwilling to wait around ten days for an outside assembler to return boards.
claims.quote_verbatim: Lumen PNP is a desktop pick and place machine. And it is intended for low to medium volume.
claims.speaker: Stephen Hawes
claims.episode_title: A Benchtop Pick and Place with Stephen Hawes

claims.claim_text: Placement-machine software is poor across the industry because switching cost locks a buyer to a fifty-thousand-dollar machine regardless of the software, and vendors compete on mechanical specifications such as transit speed and parts per hour, with a field application engineer supplied to make the software work.
claims.quote_verbatim: the cost of switching is so high. It doesn't matter how bad the software is
claims.speaker: Stephen Hawes
claims.episode_title: A Benchtop Pick and Place with Stephen Hawes

claims.claim_text: Building a desktop placement machine on an existing 3D-printer firmware stack is a deliberate reuse decision rather than a technical necessity: the motion problem is the same and the host firmware already has years of contributed work behind it.
claims.quote_verbatim: I don't want to write my own host firmware
claims.speaker: Stephen Hawes
claims.episode_title: A Benchtop Pick and Place with Stephen Hawes

claims.claim_text: The single most important calibration number on a desktop machine is the XY offset in the vision plane from the centre of the top camera's field of view to the point where the nozzle tip touches, because fiducial calibration locates the board in camera space and the nozzle must be commanded in real-world space; there are six or seven such key numbers and each machine differs by around two hundred microns.
claims.quote_verbatim: What is your X, Y offset from the center of the camera's field of view to the center of the place where the nozzle touches?
claims.speaker: Stephen Hawes
claims.episode_title: A Benchtop Pick and Place with Stephen Hawes

claims.claim_text: Powered eight-millimetre and twelve-millimetre tape feeders that identify themselves let the machine scan for all loaded feeders and remember which part is in each, so feeders can be swapped between positions without reprogramming.
claims.quote_verbatim: we have a powered feeders, eight mil, uh, eight millimeter tape and 12 millimeter tape
claims.speaker: Stephen Hawes
claims.episode_title: A Benchtop Pick and Place with Stephen Hawes

claims.claim_text: Fan-out wafer-level packaging uses a placement machine in the same role as board assembly: singulated die are placed onto double-sided adhesive tape on a steel carrier with deliberate gaps, then over-moulded in epoxy to form a reconstituted plastic wafer with a flat top surface for subsequent redistribution layers.
claims.quote_verbatim: i'm going to use a pick and place machine just like for pcbs and take all these dye and put them in some double-sided sticky tape
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Craig J Bishop

claims.claim_text: Components intended for automated assembly are supplied in tape and reel because that is the format compatible with placement machinery, which is why single-board computer modules are now sold on wide reels for machine placement.
claims.quote_verbatim: You can physically buy the thing, the complete module, on, like, a two-inch wide reel.
